extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers, and other stakeholders interested in peer-review practices and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Report and analysis of metrics used to evaluate a journal peer-review trial (eLife), comparing a trial process with the regular review process across outcomes such as acceptance rates, time to decision, editorial ratings, and demographic breakdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement rate (proportion sent for in-depth review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The encourage rate: proportion of submissions sent for in-depth review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare the trial and regular processes; earlier results reported similar encourage rates for male and female last authors in the trial (22.6% and 22.1% respectively) and higher encourage rates in the regular process (e.g., 31% for male last authors vs 28.8% for female last authors). The trial had a higher proportion of submissions rejected before peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisions after resubmission (outcomes for revised submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision outcomes for revised submissions (e.g., accepted, rejected after revision, withdrawn, pending).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 1: In the regular process, 97% of revised submissions went on to be accepted. In the trial process some revised submissions were withdrawn or remained pending at the cut-off. Black numbers in figures show submission counts; track counts of 'Revision Not Received' and withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall acceptance rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Final overall acceptance rate for submissions in each process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare regular vs trial: 14.9% of papers in the regular process accepted, compared with 20.8% in the trial process. Note that a higher pre-review rejection rate in the trial does not prevent a higher overall acceptance percentage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial ratings (degree to which review issues were addressed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three editorial ratings provided by the Reviewing Editor for trial submissions: (i) all the issues raised in the review process have been addressed in the revised version; (ii) minor issues raised in the review process remain unresolved; (iii) major issues raised in the review process remain unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to summarise quality of revisions: 88% (57/65) of accepted trial submissions were considered to have addressed all issues, 9% had minor unresolved issues (n=6), and 3% had major unresolved issues (n=2). Ratings can be published alongside peer reviews and author responses for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to first decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Elapsed time from submission to first editorial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier reports compared this measure for regular vs trial; the trial process showed slightly longer initial decision times. This is a key speed metric used alongside time to acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to acceptance (overall and by rounds of revision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Days from submission to acceptance, including medians and interquartile ranges, broken down by number of rounds of revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 4 and Table 1: median time to acceptance for submissions accepted after one round: regular 129 days vs trial 157 days. Overall median time to acceptance: regular 138 days (Q1 113, Q3 168, IQR 55); trial 175 days (Q1 129, Q3 230, IQR 101). Longer revision times in the trial account for much of the difference. One paper accepted without revisions is excluded from rounds breakdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer instruction difference (regular vs trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions given to reviewers differ by process: in the regular process reviewers are asked to consider whether requested work can be completed within two months; in the trial process reviewers are asked to comment on strengths and weaknesses and no suggested time frame is given for resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural difference affects expectations about revision scope and time-to-acceptance; it helps explain why trial revisions took longer on average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounds of revision (number of revision cycles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of revision rounds (one, two, three) and their impact on time to acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 4 shows time-to-acceptance broken down by number of rounds. Majority of accepted papers were accepted after one round, but time differs by process and by number of rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawals and pending decisions after review
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts and proportions of submissions withdrawn by authors or left pending at the cut-off point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the trial: two withdrawn, three pending at cut-off (some withdrawn after peer-review or after final rating). In the regular process: one withdrawn. Track these as outcomes distinct from accept/reject and as an indicator of author choices when given more control over publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic outcome analyses: gender of last author
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance (and encourage) rates stratified by gender of the last author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 5: In the trial, acceptance rates for male and female last authors were very similar (21% and 20.6%). In the regular process a slightly higher acceptance rate was seen for female last authors (16.8% vs 14.9% for male), but small sample sizes warrant caution. Use counts shown in bars to assess reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic outcome analyses: career stage of last author (definitions and outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance and encourage rates stratified by career stage of the last author, with definitions: early-career = independent ≤5 years; mid-career = 6–15 years; late-career = >15 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 6: earlier in trial fewer early- and mid-career submissions were encouraged for in-depth review. Final acceptance rates reported: trial — early-career 22% (vs regular 14%), mid-career 19% (vs regular 18%), late-career 32% (vs regular 20.5%). Note small-sample caveats and unexplained better performance of late-career authors in trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of removing editorial power to reject after review (non-binary outcomes and transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the trial process, the decision to reject after review was removed and publishing of peer reviews, author responses and editorial ratings was implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural change produced a range of outcomes (authors proceeding with publication even when editors judged major issues unresolved; some withdrawals). The change is presented as enabling non-binary outcomes and greater transparency; it is an evaluative dimension of the trial's design and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication format / labeling of trial papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers in the trial process have been published as Research Communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates a publication pathway/format used for the trial and can be tracked as part of outcome reporting and how trial outputs are presented to readers.
